Simple moving average.long:
The arithmetic mean of the last N closes, recalculated each bar as the window slides forward. Every bar carries equal weight: a 50-period SMA is the sum of the last fifty closes divided by fifty, nothing more.

Because it averages history it lags by construction, roughly half the window length. A new price enters at one part in N, then keeps influencing the line until it drops out N bars later, which is why an SMA can move on a day when price barely does: an old extreme just left the window.

The popular lengths - 20, 50, 200 - are conventions, not discoveries. Nothing in market structure privileges 200 days; it survived because early chartists could compute it by hand and everyone kept quoting it.

Where people get fooled: a smooth line looks like insight. The SMA contains no information beyond the closes it averages; it deletes detail rather than adding knowledge. And any crossover rule tested across enough lengths produces flattering variants by chance, because there are many lengths and only one history.
Simple moving average.usage: Plotted as a smoothed reference for recent average price, and used as the building block of crossover systems and many derived indicators.

Exponential moving average.long:
A weighted average in which the newest close receives a fixed fraction of the weight - the smoothing factor, conventionally two divided by N plus one - and the previous EMA value receives the rest. Weights decay geometrically, so recent bars dominate and old bars never fully leave; they fade.

It lags less than a simple average of the same nominal length, because recent data counts for more, but it still lags: any average of past prices sits behind the present. The quoted 'length' is a convention mapped onto the smoothing factor rather than a hard window.

Being recursive, its value depends on where the calculation began, so two platforms with different warm-up handling can draw slightly different lines from identical data.

Where people get fooled: 'less lag' gets sold as 'more predictive'. The EMA reacts faster to the last few closes, which means it also reacts faster to noise. Responsiveness and smoothness trade off directly, and the same OHLCV series sits underneath either choice.
Exponential moving average.usage: Common wherever a faster-reacting average is wanted; MACD is built from two of them.

Lag.long:
The delay between something happening in price and an indicator reflecting it. It is not a defect to be engineered away; it is the arithmetic consequence of averaging or accumulating past data. An average of the last N bars describes a period centred roughly N over two bars ago.

Every indicator built from OHLCV lags, because every one is a transformation of prices that have already printed. Oscillators, channels and so-called leading indicators differ only in how they weight and rescale that same history.

Reducing lag means weighting recent bars more heavily, which amplifies noise. The trade-off can be relocated but not removed: smooth and late, or fast and jumpy.

Where people get fooled: vendors sell 'zero-lag' tools. Mechanically these either overshoot, by extrapolating recent slope, or repaint, by revising history once later bars arrive. A signal that arrives after the move is not the indicator failing - it is averaging doing exactly what averaging of past data must do.
Lag.usage: Used as a lens for judging any smoothed indicator: how many bars behind price its message arrives.

Repainting.long:
An indicator repaints when values it plotted in the past change after later data arrives. The chart you see today is not the chart a live trader saw at the time; history has been quietly rewritten.

The mechanics are specific. Some indicators use a centred window, so the value at bar T needs bars beyond T and cannot be final until they exist. Zigzags and fractals mark a swing provisionally, then move the mark when a later bar exceeds it. Others recalculate on every tick of a forming bar, so an intrabar signal can appear and vanish before the close. Others reference a higher-timeframe bar that is still open.

In every case the finished chart keeps only the final, corrected value; each abandoned signal is erased.

Where people get fooled: replaying a repainting indicator over history shows near-perfect calls, because the losing signals no longer exist. Any backtest, screenshot or sales video built on repainted values measures hindsight, not a rule anyone could have traded.
Repainting.usage: Names the check performed before trusting a tool: confirming whether the value shown at a given bar was final when that bar closed.

Golden cross / death cross.long:
A golden cross is a shorter moving average closing above a longer one - conventionally the 50-day rising through the 200-day; a death cross is the reverse. The event is two lagged summaries of the same closing prices changing order.

Because both averages lag, the cross confirms a move long after it began. By the time a 50/200 cross prints, price has typically been moving that way for months; the cross restates the fact rather than adding to it.

The 50 and 200 lengths are conventions. Shift either one and the cross dates move by weeks, which shows the event is a property of the parameters as much as of the market.

Where people get fooled: financial media report each cross as an omen, and hindsight charts highlight the crosses that preceded big moves while the whipsaws printed in sideways markets are forgotten. A cross arriving late in a move can land near its end just as easily as its middle.
Golden cross / death cross.usage: Quoted in market commentary as a summary of long-term trend state, and used as a trigger in simple trend-following systems.

Overbought / oversold.long:
Labels applied when a bounded oscillator - RSI, stochastic, Williams %R - reaches the upper or lower end of its range. Mechanically the reading says one thing: recent closes have been persistently strong or weak relative to their own recent history. Nothing in the arithmetic measures 'too far' against any external standard.

The thresholds - 70/30 for RSI, 80/20 for the stochastic - are conventions chosen for round-number legibility, not derived from data. Change them and the frequency of 'extreme' readings changes with them.

The mean-reversion reading assumes a stretched condition snaps back. In a trending market the opposite happens: a strong trend pins the oscillator at its extreme for weeks, because the indicator is bounded and price is not.

Where people get fooled: selling something merely because an oscillator reads overbought is fading strength on the assumption that strength exhausts itself on schedule. Some of the most expensive entries available are counter-trend trades justified by an extreme reading taken during a persistent trend.
Overbought / oversold.usage: Shorthand for oscillator readings near the top or bottom of their range, commonly cited as context for fading or for waiting.

Stochastic oscillator.long:
Usually credited to George Lane. %K states where the latest close sits within the highest high and lowest low of the last N bars, scaled to a 0-100 range; %D is a short moving average of %K. It is a normalised restatement of range position, built from the same OHLCV highs and lows as everything else on the chart.

Raw %K is jumpy: a single new extreme entering or leaving the window rescales the whole reading, so one bar can jerk the line. The smoothing in %D calms it at the cost of lag - the usual exchange.

The default 14, 3, 3 settings are conventions; nothing is privileged about fourteen bars of anything, they simply became standard.

Where people get fooled: in a trend the oscillator saturates near an extreme and sits there, and each crossover back out of the zone gets read as a reversal signal when it frequently marks nothing but a pause. Divergences against price are found generously in hindsight and sparingly in advance.
Stochastic oscillator.usage: Plotted as two lines beneath the chart showing where price sits in its recent range, typically with 80/20 marked as extreme zones.

Bollinger squeeze.long:
Bollinger Bands sit a set number of standard deviations either side of a moving average, all computed from the same closes. A squeeze is the bands drawing together, which means one thing mechanically: the recent standard deviation is small. Volatility has been contracting.

The interest comes from volatility clustering - quiet spells tend to be followed by louder ones - so a squeeze is a statement about the likely size of coming movement, not its direction. Band width is backward-looking; it summarises the last N bars and knows nothing else.

Twenty periods and two standard deviations are John Bollinger's suggested defaults, retained as convention rather than validated as optimal for any particular market.

Where people get fooled: the squeeze gets traded as a directional breakout signal, and direction is precisely what it does not contain. The first move out of compression often probes one way before travelling the other, and defining 'narrowest in X bars' invites parameter shopping until history cooperates.
Bollinger squeeze.usage: Watched as a volatility filter: narrow bands flag a compressed range, usually paired with a separate directional rule.

Keltner Channel.long:
Named after Chester Keltner, whose 1960 book described a trading rule built on a ten-day average of typical price with bands based on daily range; the modern form - an exponential moving average with bands offset by a multiple of Average True Range - came later and kept his name.

The construction matters mainly by contrast with Bollinger Bands: ATR-based width responds to bar ranges rather than close-to-close standard deviation, so the channel breathes more slowly and a single outlier close distorts it less than it would the standard-deviation version.

Common settings - a 20-period EMA and twice the ATR - are conventions; both the multiplier and the lengths move the bands arbitrarily, and every derived signal moves with them.

Where people get fooled: a close outside the channel is read by some as a breakout to join and by others as an overextension to fade. The indicator supports both stories equally, which means it decides nothing by itself; it is lagged OHLCV arithmetic wearing an envelope.
Keltner Channel.usage: Drawn as a volatility envelope around an average, and a common companion to Bollinger Bands, including in squeeze definitions.

ADX.long:
The Average Directional Index, from J. Welles Wilder's 1978 New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems. In words: each bar's upward push is compared with its downward push, both are smoothed, their difference is expressed as a proportion of their sum, and that result is smoothed again into a line measuring trend strength without direction.

The double smoothing buys stability at the price of severe lag. ADX rises well after a trend is under way and falls well after it stalls, so it certifies trends that are already old and forgives ranges that have already begun.

The 14-period default is Wilder's habit carried across his indicators; the popular 20 and 25 'trending' thresholds are conventions with no derivation behind them.

Where people get fooled: a rising ADX is taken as a reason to expect persistence, yet by the time it clears the conventional threshold much of the move has already printed. And a falling ADX cannot distinguish a reversal from a rest.
ADX.usage: Used to classify market state - trending versus ranging - often as a filter that switches other rules on or off.

Ichimoku.long:
Ichimoku Kinko Hyo - roughly 'one-glance equilibrium chart' - published by the Japanese journalist Goichi Hosoda in 1969 after decades of development. Every line is a midpoint: the Tenkan and Kijun are midpoints of the last 9 and 26 bars' ranges; the cloud is built from those and a 52-bar midpoint, plotted 26 bars forward; the lagging line is the close plotted 26 bars back.

Nothing is forecast. The 'forward' cloud is past data drawn at a future x-coordinate, and midpoints of ranges lag exactly as averages do.

The 9/26/52 settings reflect the six-day Japanese trading week of Hosoda's era - 26 bars was roughly a trading month. They are historical artefacts retained as convention.

Where people get fooled: the sideways shift makes the cloud look like a prediction of future support and resistance, when it is history displaced along the axis. And five lines built from the same highs and lows generate abundant 'confluence' that is really one calculation echoing itself.
Ichimoku.usage: Displayed as a full-chart overlay whose line and cloud positions are read together as a one-glance trend summary.

Donchian Channel.long:
Named for Richard Donchian, the managed-futures pioneer who built trend-following systems on it. The construction could hardly be simpler: the upper line is the highest high of the last N bars, the lower line the lowest low, the middle their average. No smoothing, no weighting - running extremes.

The channel moves only when a new extreme prints or an old one ages out of the window, so it steps rather than glides. A breakout entry - trading beyond the prior channel - is late by design: you are buying the highest price seen in N bars, on the premise that trends persist beyond their confirmation.

Twenty bars approximates a month of daily data, which is why 20 and 55 became the famous Turtle settings; both numbers are conventions.

Where people get fooled: the clean stepped channel hides the distribution behind it. Channel-breakout systems historically depended on a few large trends paying for long strings of small losses, an experience most people abandon mid-drawdown rather than live through.
Donchian Channel.usage: Plotted as running N-bar extremes; classic breakout systems, including the Turtles', triggered on new channel highs or lows.

OBV.long:
On-Balance Volume, popularised by Joe Granville from 1963. It is a running total that adds the bar's entire volume when the close is higher than the previous close and subtracts all of it when lower. The absolute level is meaningless - it depends on the starting date - so only the slope and its divergences from price are read.

The mechanism is crude by design: a close up by one tick books the whole session's volume as 'buying', though every trade had a buyer and a seller. OBV is a transformation of close direction and volume, two columns of the same OHLCV table.

Because it accumulates, a single enormous-volume session dominates the line long afterwards, and bad volume data corrupts it silently.

Where people get fooled: divergence stories are easy to assemble in hindsight because the line has no natural scale, so whether it 'confirms' price depends on the chart window chosen. The idea that volume leads price is a hypothesis OBV assumes, not one it demonstrates.
OBV.usage: Tracked alongside price for confirmation or divergence, on the premise that shifts in volume precede shifts in price.

CCI.long:
The Commodity Channel Index, published by Donald Lambert in 1980. In words: take typical price - the average of high, low and close - subtract its own N-period average, and divide by the mean absolute deviation scaled by a constant of 0.015, which Lambert chose so that most readings land between minus 100 and plus 100.

So it measures how far price sits from its recent average, in units of its own recent variability - a z-score-like oscillator. Despite the reference lines it is unbounded, and despite the name there is nothing commodity-specific in the formula.

The 20-period default and the plus-and-minus-100 thresholds are conventions, nothing more.

Where people get fooled: the reference lines look like boundaries, but strong trends push the index far beyond them and hold it there. The same reading is taught contradictorily - above plus 100 as a momentum entry in one school, an overbought warning in another - which is a sign the number decides less than its users do.
CCI.usage: Read as an oscillator showing displacement from the recent mean, with the plus-and-minus-100 lines used as conventional extreme markers.

Williams %R.long:
Larry Williams' %R states where the latest close sits relative to the range of the last N bars, scaled from zero at the range high to minus 100 at the range low. Arithmetically it is the stochastic %K inverted and shifted; the two lines contain identical information.

As pure range position it rescales whenever a new extreme enters or leaves the lookback window, so a single bar can jerk the reading, and Williams' version plots raw where the stochastic convention adds smoothing - faster, and jumpier, by the same amount.

The 14-period default and the minus-20 and minus-80 extreme zones are conventions mirroring the stochastic's 80/20; none of the numbers is derived from anything beyond habit.

Where people get fooled: adding %R to a chart that already carries a stochastic or RSI feels like a second opinion, but it is the same opinion with a different sign convention. Counting 'three oscillators agree' as confirmation is counting one calculation three times.
Williams %R.usage: Plotted as a bounded oscillator of range position, effectively an inverted and unsmoothed stochastic %K.

SuperTrend.long:
A trailing line plotted a chosen multiple of Average True Range away from a midpoint price: below price while the state is up, above it while the state is down. When price closes through the line, the line flips to the other side. It is an ATR trailing stop packaged as an indicator and coloured for legibility.

The flip lags any turn by however far the band sits from price - that distance is the whole design. In ranges the line is forever chasing a price that keeps doubling back, so repeated flips are structural, not bad luck.

The common 10-period, three-times-ATR settings are conventions; widening the multiplier trades fewer whipsaws for later exits, and no setting escapes that trade-off.

Where people get fooled: the coloured ribbon on a historical chart looks like a machine that caught every trend. Each flip printed after the move that caused it, and the sideways stretches - where markets spend most of their time - produced strings of losing flips the eye skates past.
SuperTrend.usage: Displayed as a flipping trailing line, used as a trend-state marker or as a ready-made trailing stop.

Parabolic SAR.long:
From J. Welles Wilder's 1978 book: 'stop and reverse'. A dot trails price from the recent extreme and accelerates towards it each bar the move extends, the acceleration factor rising in steps to a cap. When price touches the dot, the position is stopped out and reversed, and the dots restart on the other side.

It assumes you are always in the market, long or short, and it was designed for sustained trends: the tightening action exits parabolic moves close to their extremes and gets chopped without mercy in ranges. Wilder himself paired it with a trend filter for exactly that reason.

The 0.02 step and 0.20 maximum are Wilder's suggested settings, conventions ever since, with no special standing.

Where people get fooled: on a trending chart the dots look prescient. In a range the always-in construction makes every false flip cost twice - the exit and the wrong-way entry. Obeying the dots selectively reintroduces all the discretion the tool advertised removing.
Parabolic SAR.usage: Plotted as dots above or below price and used as a trailing stop, or as the always-in reversal system Wilder designed.

Pivot points.long:
The classic floor-trader pivot is the average of the previous session's high, low and close; the surrounding support and resistance levels are arithmetic reflections around it. Camarilla, Woodie and Fibonacci variants change the formulas but not the inputs - everything derives from three numbers fixed before the session opens.

That fixity is a genuine virtue: pivots cannot repaint and involve no smoothing, so there is no lag in the usual sense. They are yesterday's range projected forward, nothing subtler.

Any tendency for price to react around them would have to come from behaviour - enough participants watching the same levels that orders cluster there. That is a testable behavioural mechanism, not a property of the arithmetic itself.

Where people get fooled: with a pivot plus three supports and three resistances drawn, price is nearly always near some level, so the levels seem respected - touches are memorable and misses invisible. Judged by eye, that asymmetry does all of the work.
Pivot points.usage: Calculated before the session from the prior day's high, low and close, and watched intraday as reference levels.

Heikin Ashi.long:
Synthetic candles, from the Japanese for roughly 'average bar'. Each Heikin Ashi close is the average of the real bar's open, high, low and close; each open is the average of the previous synthetic candle's open and close; the plotted highs and lows are the extremes of the real high, the real low and the synthetic body. The smoothing is recursive - every candle inherits its predecessor.

Be precise about what is discarded: the true open and close of every bar are gone; gaps vanish, because each candle is forced to open inside the previous synthetic body; and the plotted values are prices at which no trade may ever have occurred.

The result is long runs of same-coloured candles in trends, which is exactly why the chart looks calm.

Where people get fooled: backtesting fills at Heikin Ashi prices books trades at prices that never existed, flattering every result. And the smoothness that hides noise also hides the bar that would have shown the trend ending.
Heikin Ashi.usage: Charted in place of ordinary candles to make trend phases visually cleaner, often alongside a normal chart for actual prices.

Renko.long:
A chart of bricks, each a fixed size in price terms - points, or an ATR-derived amount. A new brick prints only when price travels a full brick beyond the last one's edge; a reversal conventionally requires two bricks' worth. The horizontal axis counts bricks, not time.

Be precise about what is discarded: time, since a brick may take a minute or a week to form; volume; and the path inside a brick, so wicks, failed probes and the order of intrabar highs and lows all vanish. Bricks print only on completion, so every signal arrives at least a full brick after the move that caused it.

Brick size is the single parameter, and the chart's entire character depends on it - halve it and a calm staircase becomes a ragged mess.

Where people get fooled: Renko backtests flatter, because assuming fills at exact brick boundaries hides slippage and the adverse movement inside bricks. A strategy that looks serene on bricks can be untradeable on the underlying prices.
Renko.usage: Used as an alternative chart type that filters out moves smaller than the brick size, redrawing price as equal-sized steps.

Market profile.long:
Developed by Peter Steidlmayer at the Chicago Board of Trade in the 1980s. Each session's trading is arranged as a distribution over price: how much time, or volume, the market spent at each level. The most-visited price is the point of control; the region holding roughly seventy per cent of activity is, by convention, the value area.

It is a description of an auction. Fat regions of the profile show where two-sided trade found acceptance; thin tails show where price was rejected quickly. A bell shape records balance; an elongated profile records a directional, imbalanced session.

None of this forecasts anything. Prior value areas and points of control are reference levels for framing the next session; any predictive claim about them is a separate hypothesis needing its own test.

Where people get fooled: the auction vocabulary sounds explanatory, and users slide from 'value was there yesterday' to treating the value area as a magnet. The profile summarises what happened; 'markets return to value' is an assumption the reader imports.
Market profile.usage: Displayed as a per-session distribution of activity at price, supplying reference levels such as the point of control and value area.

Indicator stacking.long:
Requiring several indicators to agree before acting - RSI plus MACD plus a stochastic plus a moving average - on the theory that agreement is confirmation. The stack usually grows one disappointment at a time, each new tool added to filter the failures of the last.

The mechanical objection: every one of them is a transformation of the same OHLCV series. RSI, the stochastic, Williams %R and CCI are all rescalings of recent closes against recent range or mean; MACD is two exponential averages of the same closes. When they agree, they mostly agree because they share inputs. That is correlated redundancy, not independent evidence.

Each added indicator also adds parameters, multiplying the ways a backtest can be tuned until it flatters - researcher degrees of freedom dressed up as rigour.

Where people get fooled: five agreeing panels feel like five witnesses; it is closer to one witness holding five microphones. Genuine confirmation requires an input the first indicator does not already contain - different data, not a different formula over the same bars.
Indicator stacking.usage: Describes chart setups where multiple indicators must align before a trade is taken.

Parameter choice.long:
Every indicator carries numbers someone chose: 14 for RSI and ADX (Wilder's habit), 20 and 2 for Bollinger Bands, 9/26/52 for Ichimoku (a relic of six-day trading weeks), 12/26/9 for MACD. None was derived from evidence that still binds; they were computational conveniences and personal defaults that hardened into standards.

Mechanically, a parameter sets a window on the same OHLCV data: longer means smoother and later, shorter means noisier and sooner. There is no correct length, because the trade-off is continuous and shifts with market regime.

A more honest question than 'what is the best setting' is whether performance survives in the neighbourhood: if 14 works while 12 and 17 do not, the result is probably noise wearing a number.

Where people get fooled: optimising parameters over history is a search across noise, and the best-looking setting is best partly by luck, so it degrades live. Defaults have one virtue - they were not fitted to your own test data.
Parameter choice.usage: Refers to the settings an indicator needs before it produces a value, and to how those settings are selected or justified.
